engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

book.author: Eric Ries
book.chapter: Build-Measure-Learn: Stop Building What Nobody Wants
book.lesson: The biggest waste in startups — and in corporate innovation — is building products nobody wants. Ries's solution: the Build-Measure-Learn loop. Start with a hypothesis about what customers want. Build the minimum viable product (MVP) to test it — not a polished product, just enough to learn. Measure how real customers actually behave. Learn whether your hypothesis was right. Pivot or persevere based on evidence, not ego. The goal is to minimise the total time through the loop. Most teams optimise for building fast. They should optimise for learning fast.
book.key_quote: Speed of learning, not speed of building, is the true competitive advantage of innovative teams.
book.action: Identify one assumption behind your current project. What is the cheapest, fastest test you could run to validate or invalidate it this week?
crux: A startup is an organisation built to find a repeatable business model under extreme uncertainty.
Build–Measure–Learn. Speed through the loop is the core competency.
Validated learning is the unit of progress, not code shipped or hours worked.
Minimum Viable Product: the smallest thing that tests the riskiest assumption.
Two leap-of-faith assumptions: value (do they want it?) and growth (how does it spread?).
Genchi genbutsu — go and see. Talk to actual users, not to your model of them.
Vanity metrics (totals, page views) flatter. Actionable metrics (cohort retention, conversion) inform.
Cohort analysis and split testing are the only honest reads on whether you improved anything.
Innovation accounting: define the baseline, tune the engine, then pivot or persevere.
Three growth engines: sticky (retention), viral (referral), paid (unit economics). Pick one.
Pivot types: zoom-in, zoom-out, customer segment, platform, business architecture, value capture.
Small batches expose problems immediately. Large batches hide them until launch.
Stop the line — fix root causes with five whys rather than shipping over them.
The question is never 'can we build this?' It is 'should we build this?'
learnings: Shipping is not progress. Learning is progress.
Most feature work is waste because most assumptions are wrong.
A metric that only goes up is not telling you anything.
Deciding to pivot late is the expensive part, not the pivot itself.
examples: Dropbox tested demand with a 3-minute video before building sync. Beta waitlist went 5,000 → 75,000 overnight.
Zappos began by photographing shoes in local shops and buying at retail per order — testing willingness to buy online before holding inventory.
Ries's IMVU spent months on an IM-interoperability feature nobody used. Users didn't want to add friends; they wanted new ones.
adapt: Codex at $47: test the tier with a landing page and real payment intent before building the full product.
The signal edge measurement was validated learning — t=+2.87 on daily equity, noise on 1H. That result should drive the roadmap.
Cohort the newspaper: are the same readers returning, or is it new traffic each morning? Totals won't tell you.
Five whys on the alert flood: no time stop → because no lifecycle rule → because the backtest's horizon was never ported to live code.

interview_tech.q: Explain covenant headroom and how you monitor it.
interview_tech.a: Covenants are contractual ratios — typically net debt to EBITDA, interest cover, and sometimes minimum net worth — tested quarterly. Headroom is the distance between your forecast ratio and the limit. Monitor it forward, not backward: run the covenant calculation inside the rolling forecast so you see a breach two quarters out while you can still act. Post-IFRS 16, check whether the definitions are frozen GAAP or current GAAP — lease liabilities entering net debt has breached covenants that had nothing to do with performance.

interview_tech.q: What controls matter most in a 60-store retail environment?
interview_tech.a: Rank by exposure. Cash and tender reconciliation daily at store level with independent review; goods receiving matched three-way to purchase order and invoice, because that is where margin leaks; inventory counts on a rolling cycle rather than one annual heroic count; markdown authorisation limits by role; and user access in the ERP reviewed quarterly, especially for leavers. Segregation of duties is hardest at small stores — compensate with detective controls and exception reporting rather than pretending it exists.

interview_soft.q: How do you stay current technically while managing?
interview_soft.a: Be specific and verifiable. Name the standard you last read in full and why, the technical update you attended, the thing you built yourself recently rather than delegated. Vague answers about 'reading widely' land badly with technical interviewers. The strongest version connects it to a decision: 'I went back through IFRS 16 properly when we hit the lease modification question on the Indonesian stores, and that changed how we structured the renewal.'

interview_soft.q: Where do you think retail is heading in the next five years?
interview_soft.a: Have a view and defend it with numbers, not trends. Something like: physical stores stop being judged on their own sales as fulfilment and returns blur the channels, which breaks conventional store P&L and forces a catchment-level view; margin pressure shifts from price to cost-to-serve; and in the Gulf specifically, corporate tax and e-invoicing professionalise finance functions that were previously light. Then say what you would do about it in the role you are interviewing for.

cfo_field.q: Learn the lease standard properly. In the Gulf it is not a footnote.
cfo_field.a: IFRS 16 put every store lease on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. Two consequences a CFO must be able to say out loud: EBITDA is now flattered, because rent that used to sit in operating costs is split into depreciation and interest; and leverage ratios move even though nothing about the business changed. If your covenant is set on a pre-IFRS-16 basis, know it before the bank asks.

cfo_field.q: Automation without a control map is how a finance function loses its audit trail.
cfo_field.a: Before automating a process, write down: who can initiate, who approves, what the system does without a human, and where the exception report goes. Automation does not remove controls; it moves them from people to configuration, and configuration drifts silently. The question 'what breaks if this runs wrong for a month before anyone notices' is the one that separates a finance automation from a finance incident.
